52883.headline: ABCA now resolves the attester key from a trusted `x5c` chain, ready to merge.
52883.summary: The PR lets `findAttesterKey` take the attester key from the `x5c` header. It validates the chain against the X.509 trust anchors of the client's `attester_trust_idps`, and it keeps the `kid` lookup for JWKS-only setups. It reuses the same `TrustMaterialResolver.validateX509Chain` path that key attestations already use. Rejections map to `invalid_client_attestation`, and the tests cover the trusted chain, the untrusted chain and the `kid` fallback.
52883.eudi: EUDI and HAIP wallets that send their Wallet Attestation with an `x5c` chain and no `kid` can now authenticate at the token endpoint against a Wallet Provider CA. Revocation of the Wallet Provider certificate is still not checked, which is a limit of the existing validator and not of this PR.
good: The change reuses the existing chain validator and trust provider contract instead of adding a second X.509 path.
A configured chain that fails validation throws and never falls back to `kid`, so a bad `x5c` cannot be rescued by a JWKS key.
The x5c tests clear the `kid`, so they really cover the case from #52766.

findings.title: An attestation without `x5c` skips X.509 trust and goes straight to the `kid` lookup.
findings.impact: A client that lists an X.509 trust provider next to a JWKS provider accepts a `kid`-only attestation from the JWKS provider, even though the X.509 provider says a chain is mandatory.
findings.detail: dominikschlosser raised this in a comment and the code still has it. `validateX509Chain` only runs when `x5c` is present. The `TrustMaterialIdentityProvider` contract says that exposing X.509 trust anchors makes chain validation mandatory and that a missing chain fails. The harm is limited, because the JWKS provider is itself trusted by the admin and a single X.509 provider returns no keys from `resolveKeys`. The key attestation path in `AttestationValidatorUtil` has the same shape, so this PR does not make it worse.
findings.fix: Call `validateX509Chain` for every attestation, also when `x5c` is absent. It then throws when X.509 trust is configured and no chain is sent, and returns `null` for JWKS-only setups, so the `kid` fallback still works there. Apply the same change to the key attestation path.

54522.headline: Sound fail closed ETSI LoTE trust provider with only small docs and validation gaps.
54522.summary: The PR adds an `etsi-trust-list` identity provider that downloads a signed ETSI TS 119 602 LoTE, verifies it against pinned signing certificates, checks `LoTEType`, service type, service status and `NextUpdate`, and exposes the listed CA certificates as X.509 trust anchors. It also lets `X509TrustMaterial` accept subordinate CAs as anchors. Load failures, expired lists and discontinued lists all lead to no trust material from this provider without breaking other providers, and the tests cover these cases. What remains are a misleading validation message, one missing docs sentence, a missing forced reload and a test with a real list shape.
54522.eudi: Keycloak can now use EUDI Wallet Provider, PID Provider and PubEAA Provider LoTEs directly for key attestations and SD-JWT VC presentations, but not yet for client attestations, which still need the `x5c` support from #52883. Admins must pin the list signing certificates and update them on rotation, because the provider does not follow a List of Trusted Lists yet.
good: Every failure path fails closed for this provider only. `listedCertificates` catches load errors so other trust providers of the client still work, and `unavailableListDoesNotBlockOtherTrustProviders` tests this.
The cache entry expires at the earlier of the refresh interval and `NextUpdate`, and a list without `NextUpdate` is treated as discontinued as clause 6.3.15 requires.
The anchor filter in `isCaCertificate` matches the checks in the `X509TrustMaterial` constructor. One unusable CA on a list therefore cannot make the whole list throw.

findings.title: The provider does not override `reloadKeys()`, so the reload keys endpoint cannot force a new download.
findings.impact: When the scheme operator withdraws a compromised wallet provider CA, Keycloak trusts it for up to the refresh interval unless the admin knows that saving the provider clears the cache.
findings.detail: `IdentityProvider.reloadKeys()` defaults to false, while Default Trust, OIDC and SAML override it. Saving the provider publishes `IdentityProviderUpdatedEvent`, and that event clears the cache entry, so a workaround exists. Awambeng raised this.
findings.fix: Override `reloadKeys()` to call `PublicKeyStorageProvider.reloadKeys(modelKey, new EtsiTrustListPublicKeyLoader(session, config))` with the same model key as `listedCertificates()`.

findings.title: An empty signing certificate field reports an invalid PEM bundle instead of a missing certificate.
findings.impact: An admin who leaves the field empty gets a misleading error message, but the configuration is still rejected.
findings.detail: The `isEmpty()` check throws inside the `try`, and the `catch (RuntimeException e)` wraps that exception in the PEM bundle message. Awambeng raised this.
findings.fix: Decode the certificates inside the `try` and check `isEmpty()` after the `catch`.

findings.title: The docs do not say that an empty status setting ignores all services that carry a status.
findings.impact: An admin who configures a PubEAA list without statuses gets no trust anchors and cannot see why from the docs or the log.
findings.detail: `toKeys` keeps a service with a status only when the status is configured, and it drops the other services without a log line. The author says the missing default is on purpose, and `servicesWithAStatusAreIgnoredWithoutConfiguredStatuses` tests it. The docs and the help text only say that services without a status are always trusted. The EKU setting on the same page at line 113 uses the opposite rule, where an empty list means no restriction. Awambeng raised this.

54367.headline: Correct jti replay and iat freshness checks for ABCA PoP, matching DPoP.
54367.summary: The PR rejects Client Attestation PoP JWTs whose `iat` falls outside a 10s lifetime plus 15s skew window, and it records each PoP `jti` in `SingleUseObjectProvider` so a second use fails. The replay entry is written only after the signature check, and its key carries a namespace, the realm id, the `jti` and the client id. The lifespan covers the whole accepted window and is never zero. The checks are sound and the tests cover the main behaviour.
54367.eudi: A wallet that builds a fresh PoP for every PAR, token and refresh request keeps working, and a captured PoP can no longer be replayed. A wallet that reuses one PoP across requests, or whose clock is more than 15 seconds ahead or about 25 seconds behind, is now rejected, and the server challenge that would remove the clock dependency is still missing.
good: The replay entry is written after the PoP signature is verified, so unauthenticated requests cannot use up `jti` values.
The cache key is namespaced by `abca-pop`, the realm id and the issuer, and the lifespan is clamped to at least one second.
The HAIP conformance tests now mint a fresh PoP for each token and refresh request.

findings.title: No test replays a PoP near the end of its accepted window.
findings.impact: A later edit to the lifespan arithmetic could let a captured PoP be replayed between second 10 and second 25 after `iat`, and no test would notice.
findings.detail: Copilot raised this in review and the tests still lack it. `testClientAttestationPoPReplayRejected` replays right away, so it would still pass if the cache entry expired after only `DEFAULT_POP_LIFETIME_SECONDS`. The current code is correct. The gap is that nothing pins it down. No test covers an `iat` in the future within the skew either.
findings.fix: Add a test that builds a PoP with `iat` about 10 seconds in the past, uses it once, pauses about 3 seconds and checks that the replay fails with `already been used`. Keep the `iat` well away from the 25 second limit, because the browser logins between the two requests eat into the window. Add one case with `iat` slightly in the future.

discussion.answer: The fixed window is deliberate and equals the DPoP window, which `DPoPUtil.Validator` also sets from constants without a setter. A HAIP wallet whose clock is outside that window already fails the DPoP check on the same token request, so a setting for ABCA alone gains little. The remedy the ABCA draft offers for bad device clocks is the server challenge, which the description leaves for a later PR.

54282.headline: Mapper-inferred DCQL works and is validated. Optional claims are a follow-up.
54282.summary: The PR builds the DCQL query from the claim paths of the OID4VP mappers, the configured `vct` values and the principal attribute. A hand-written query still takes precedence, and it is now parsed into a typed model and validated when the identity provider is saved. Request object build failures are still caught and turned into an error page, and existing providers with a working query keep working. I found nothing that must change before merge.
54282.eudi: EUDI verifiers can list several national PID types such as `urn:eudi:pid:de:1` and `urn:eudi:pid:it:1` and get a valid single credential query without writing DCQL. Every mapped claim is requested as mandatory, so mappers for optional PID attributes still need a hand-written query with `claim_sets`.
good: The typed `DcqlQuery` model rejects unknown members, null entries and queries the response handling cannot serve, so admins see HTTP 400 on save instead of a failing login.
Mappers without a target attribute no longer add claims to the inferred query, so unused mappers do not block wallets.
The integration tests cover inference, override precedence, `vct` deduplication and each validation error message.

findings.title: Every mapped claim is requested as mandatory, with no way to mark a mapper claim optional.
findings.impact: An admin maps the optional PID attribute `email` to the user email, and holders whose PID has no `email` cannot log in because the wallet finds no matching credential.
findings.detail: The inferred query lists all mapper claims without `claim_sets`, so OID4VP 1.0 §6.4.1 requires the wallet to return all of them or no credential. The mappers themselves tolerate an absent claim, and the ARF PID rulebook makes attributes such as `email`, `address` and `nationalities` optional. With the inferred query an absent optional attribute now fails the whole login. The workaround is a hand-written query with `claim_sets`, which defeats the point of inference for common PID setups.
findings.fix: Add a per mapper required flag, defaulting to required, and emit `claim_sets` that always contain the required claims and the principal and optionally the optional claims. Until then, mention in the help text and release notes that every mapped claim must be present in the credential.
context: * The name of the attribute the claim is stored in, null if none is configured.

53652.headline: Small, correct bulk revocation of issued credentials per wallet client with indexes and tests.
53652.summary: The PR adds `DELETE /admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{id}/vc/issued-credentials`, which deletes every issued credential record of one wallet client in local and federated storage. It reuses the `deleteIssuedVcsByClient` and `deleteFederatedIssuedVcsByClient` queries that client removal already runs, and it adds `CLIENT_ID` indexes on both tables. `OID4VCIRefreshTokenProvider.validateToken` calls `OID4VCUtil.checkIssuedVerifiableCredential`, which fails when the record is gone, so the deletion really blocks further refreshes. I found nothing that must change.
53652.eudi: Issuers get a single call to stop credential refresh for every user of a compromised wallet application. The call works per OAuth client and not per wallet unit, and credentials that wallets already hold stay valid until `exp`, so the revocation that the ARF expects from a PID provider still needs a status list.
good: The endpoint reuses the delete queries that client removal already uses, so bulk revoke and client deletion behave the same way.
The plain `createIndex` changesets go through `CustomCreateIndexChange`, which overrides `createIndex`, so the 300000 row threshold described in the upgrade note really applies to both new indexes.
The endpoint requires `manage` on the client. That adds no privilege because the same caller can already delete the client and with it all issued credential records.

changes: I shortened the summary from five to four sentences and named `OID4VCIRefreshTokenProvider.validateToken` as the caller of the check, because the format allows at most four sentences.
I rewrote the `eudi` text, because the endpoint works per OAuth client for all its users and only stops refresh, so it is not the wallet unit revocation response that the ARF expects.

53645.headline: Clean bulk revoke endpoints that reuse existing deletion queries and match single revoke semantics.
53645.summary: The PR adds an admin endpoint and an account endpoint that delete all issued credential records of one user. It adds a `removeIssuedVerifiableCredentials` model operation that routes local users to `deleteIssuedVcsByUser` and federated users to the realm scoped `deleteFederatedIssuedVcsByUser`, and reuses it in the user removal paths without changing their behaviour. Authorization, feature checks, CORS and admin events match the existing single credential revoke endpoints, and tests cover isolation from other users, idempotency, both account roles, the 403 case and federated users. I found nothing that must change.
53645.eudi: Issuers can now cut off credential refresh for a whole user in one call, for example after a lost wallet, because the refresh token provider rejects refresh when the issued record is gone. Credentials already held by wallets stay valid until they expire, since this PR does not touch any status list.
good: The new operation reuses the existing bulk JPA queries and the user deletion paths now call it, so there is one deletion path per storage type.
The account endpoint acts only on the authenticated user, and tests check that another user's records survive.
The docs state clearly that entitlements stay and that refresh of removed records stops.

50897.headline: The new `target_client` rule is undocumented and the documented pre-authorized call now fails.
50897.summary: The PR adds a `target_client` parameter to `create-credential-offer` and stops binding pre-authorized offers to the client that created them. When `target_client` is omitted, the provider discovers the single enabled OID4VCI client that holds all requested credential scopes, and explicit targets are checked for those scopes. The validation and the tests are solid, including cross-client creation and redemption after the client is disabled. The discovery rule is deliberate, but the PR changes no docs, so the documented pre-authorized call now fails in the setup that the same docs describe.
50897.eudi: EUDI issuers that register several wallet clients with the same PID or attestation scope cannot rely on discovery. Their issuer portal must pass `target_client` on every pre-authorized offer call.
good: Explicit targets are now checked against the optional credential scopes at offer time, so a misconfigured client fails at creation and not later at the credential endpoint.
The test matrices cover a creator client without scopes that targets a different issuance client, and they run through to an issued credential.
Credential scope lookup happens once, before the offer state is built, and the discovered client is written to the event and the logs.

53046.headline: Generated EC certificates are now persisted, so JWKS and issuer x5c values stay stable.
53046.summary: The PR moves self-signed certificate generation for `ecdsa-generated` and `ecdh-generated` providers into `AbstractGeneratedEcKeyProviderFactory#validateConfiguration`, so the certificate is stored with the component like in the RSA generated provider. A key regeneration after a curve change drops the old certificate and issues a new one. Admin updates cannot clear or overwrite the stored certificate because `RepresentationToModel#updateComponent` ignores config keys that are not declared properties, and realm import also runs `validateConfiguration`. The validity period stays at ten years as before, and the three integration tests cover the main lifecycle cases.
53046.eudi: Realms that enable `ecGenerateCertificate` on a generated EC key now publish the same `x5c` and `x5t` in the JWKS and in the header of signed credential issuer metadata on every node and after restarts. SD-JWT VC issuance does not change, because `SdJwtCredentialSigner#addHaipX5cHeader` rejects a self-signed signing certificate, and as the author says, components created before the upgrade keep the old per-instance certificate until an admin saves them once.
good: The fix mirrors the established RSA generated provider and persists the certificate in one place that runs on create, update and import.
A curve change removes the stale certificate inside `generateKeys`, so a certificate can never describe a different key pair.
The tests check stability across component reloads, enabling the option on an existing key, and regeneration after a curve change.

changes: Corrected the `eudi` text, because `SdJwtCredentialSigner#addHaipX5cHeader` throws for a self-signed signing certificate, so the stable certificate reaches the JWKS and the signed issuer metadata but not SD-JWT VCs.

44207.headline: The typed KB-JWT payload and the `alg: none` rejection are sound and only nits remain.
44207.summary: The PR makes `SdJws` generic and adds a typed `KeyBindingPayload`. `KeyBindingJWT` always signs with `typ` set to `kb+jwt`, and the verifier now rejects a KB-JWT whose header has `alg` set to `none` or no `alg`. Valid presentations verify as before, the new rejection has a test, and I found no leftover use of the removed or renamed APIs in the files I read. Nothing must change before merge, but the four small points from tnorimat are still in the code and the branch still carries the commits of the merged constants PR.
44207.eudi: Verifiers built on this SDK now reject unsigned KB-JWTs explicitly, as RFC 9901 Section 7.3 requires and HAIP 1.0 relies on for holder binding. Issuance output is unchanged because the service side changes only move constants.
good: `validateKeyBindingAlgorithm` rejects `none` before signature checking, and `testShouldFail_IfAlgorithmNone` covers it with a real test vector.
`KeyBindingJWT.from` no longer takes a `jwsType`, so callers cannot sign a KB-JWT with a wrong `typ`.
`KeyBindingPayload` replaces untyped `JsonNode` access with named getters, and `@JsonAnySetter` keeps extra claims intact.

findings.impact: An operator who debugs a rejected presentation with no `alg` header sees a message that blames `none`.
findings.detail: `validateKeyBindingAlgorithm` throws the same text for `alg == null` and for `Algorithm.none`, so a missing header is reported as `incorrect algorithm 'none'`.
findings.fix: Put the actual `alg` value in the message, or use a separate message when the header has no `alg`.
context: throw new VerificationException("Key Binding JWT has incorrect algorithm '" + Algorithm.none + "'");

53476.headline: The opt-in check that the proof key is attested_keys[0] is correct and backward compatible.
53476.summary: The PR adds the optional `vc.key_attestation.proof_key_index` scope attribute. When it is set to 0, a JWT proof is accepted only if its signing key is `attested_keys[0]`. Without it, the existing membership check stays as it was. The admin create and update paths and realm import reject any value other than 0 with HTTP 400, so a bad value cannot reach `SupportedCredentialConfiguration.parse` and break issuer metadata for the whole realm. The two gaps that remain were raised by dominikschlosser, already existed before this PR and are tracked in issue 54634.
53476.eudi: EUDI issuers can now enforce the ETSI TS 119 472-3 rule that the JWT proof key is `attested_keys[0]`. Wallets that send `kid` as a position in `attested_keys`, like the EUDI reference wallet, are still rejected before this check runs.
good: The default membership check is unchanged, so existing configurations keep working.
`validateProofKeyIndex` uses the same parsing as the model getter, so values that would break metadata are rejected with HTTP 400 before they are stored.
Unit tests cover the accept and reject cases with and without a required index, and the error message names the index where the key was found.

This existed before the PR. It matters more now because wallets that follow ETSI are the main users of the new option. The author tracks it in issue 54634.

53332.headline: Per user issued credential cache with sound cluster invalidation, ready to merge.
53332.summary: The PR caches each user's issued verifiable credentials in the user cache and invalidates the entry on add, remove, user credential removal, user and realm invalidation, and expired row cleanup. Expired row cleanup uses a global invalidation revision that is bumped only when rows were actually removed, and the new count method keeps the old `void` cleanup contract through a default method. I traced the storage paths that delete issued credential rows and each one reaches a per user, realm or global invalidation. The global flush is wider than needed in two places, which costs cache hits but not correctness.
53332.eudi: Wallets that come back within one cleanup interval put less load on the database, because the issued credential lookup in `OID4VCUtil.checkIssuedVerifiableCredential` is now served from cache. Removing an issued credential invalidates the owner's entry on every node once the transaction completes, so a revoked credential is not refreshed from a stale entry beyond the usual short delay of cluster invalidation.
good: The unscoped `removeIssuedVerifiableCredential(credentialId)` resolves the owner first and then uses the owner scoped delete, so the right user's entry is invalidated.
The global invalidation revision is checked against each cached entry, so a load that races with expired row cleanup cannot keep stale data.
The new `removeExpiredIssuedVerifiableCredentialsWithCount` is a default method that returns `-1` and falls back to invalidation, so existing providers keep working.

findings.title: Expired row cleanup flushes every cached entry whenever one row expired.
findings.impact: On an issuer with steady issuance, some credential expires in almost every 15 minute cleanup interval, so every run makes all nodes reload every user's issued credentials.
findings.detail: `removeExpiredIssuedVerifiableCredentialsWithCount` calls `invalidateAllIssuedVerifiableCredentials()` when any row was deleted, and that bumps the revision that every cached entry is compared against. After the bump the first read per user is not cached again, because `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` in `getIssuedVerifiableCredentialsStreamByUser` raises the key revision above the `startupRevision` of the reading session and `addRevisioned` then skips the put. The result stays correct, but a cached entry lives 15 minutes at most on a busy system. A wallet that refreshes less often than that gets no benefit from the cache.
findings.fix: In a later PR, invalidate only the owners of the expired rows, for example by selecting their user IDs before the delete. Another option is to leave the cache alone on cleanup and filter expired entries when reading.

53415.headline: Sound fix for custom JWS algorithms, but attacker chosen alg strings now reach WARN logs.
53415.summary: The PR stores the JWS `alg` header as a string so tokens signed by a custom `SignatureProvider` parse, and it switches the service verification paths from `getAlgorithm().name()` to `getRawAlgorithm()`. I read every changed path and the enum callers that remain in `TokenVerifier` and the CIBA request parser. They fail closed on an unknown or missing `alg`, because provider lookups by id return null, `CryptoUtils.getSignatureProvider` rejects null, and `DefaultKeycloakSession.getProvider` throws on a null id. The one new exposure is that unauthenticated endpoints now log any `alg` string at WARN.
53415.eudi: OID4VCI proof and attestation checks and the OID4VP `ACCEPTED_ALGORITHMS` check still gate on allow lists, so HAIP algorithm restrictions are unchanged. Custom or PQC signature providers become usable for proofs and attestations once they are registered and the issuer configuration allows them.

Every changed provider lookup keeps an explicit rejection of a missing `alg` instead of relying on an NPE.
Header serialization is byte for byte unchanged and `JWSHeaderTest` pins it for known and custom algorithms.

The userinfo bearer token, the client registration token and the organization invitation token need no authentication. A JSON string such as `"x\nINFO [org.keycloak.events] type=LOGIN ..."` is logged as is. The WARN line itself is not new, since an enum name without a provider such as `none` already reached it. 53531.headline: Opt-in HAIP trust anchor rejection is correctly scoped to key attestations and well tested.
53531.summary: The PR adds a `rejectTrustAnchorInX5c` option to the Default Trust provider. When the option is on, a key-attestation `x5c` chain that contains a configured trust anchor is rejected. A new `TrustMaterialRequest.Purpose` limits the policy to `KEY_ATTESTATION` requests, so OID4VP SD-JWT issuer validation and client attestation keep their current behaviour. The option is off by default, existing stored configs read as `false`, and both the direct `attestation` proof and the `key_attestation` embedded in a JWT proof are tested.
53531.eudi: EUDI issuers can now enforce the HAIP 1.0 rule that wallets leave the trust anchor out of the key-attestation `x5c` header. Trust still comes only from the configured roots, so turning the option on makes the check stricter without widening what is trusted.
good: The policy is carried per trust material, so roots and settings from different providers are never mixed.
Scoping by request purpose keeps OID4VP issuer `x5c` validation unchanged when the option is enabled.
Tests cover the rejected and accepted cases for both proof types and check the specific error message.

53588.headline: The derived idle timeout equals the refresh interval for intervals of 30 days or more.
53588.summary: The PR caps each OID4VCI refresh token at the smaller of the credential expiry and a configurable idle timeout, which restarts on every refresh. It validates the chain of refresh interval, idle timeout and credential lifetime against the merged state on update, and it keeps the rotation record until the latest expiry in the token family. The code matches the description and the earlier review points are fixed. One gap should be closed here: the derived default and the validation allow an idle timeout equal to the refresh interval, and then the refresh token expires just before the credential it should renew.
53588.eudi: EUDI issuers get a bounded refresh token by default, so a wallet that is lost or stops refreshing loses refresh rights after 30 days instead of after the full credential lifetime. Issuers with a refresh interval of 30 days or more should set an explicit idle timeout above the interval until the default leaves slack.
good: The rotation record keeps the maximum family expiry and carries it forward, so lowering the idle timeout cannot reopen replay of a consumed parent token.
`ClientScopeResource.update` now applies protocol defaults first and validates the merged state that is actually persisted.
The tests cover idle expiry, restart on refresh, the derived default, partial updates and replay after descendants expire.

findings.title: The derived idle timeout equals the refresh interval when the interval is 30 days or more.
findings.impact: An issuer with a refresh interval of 30 days or more gets wallets that fail with `invalid_grant` when they refresh once the credential has expired, also for existing scopes after the upgrade.
findings.detail: The default is `max(min(30 days, lifetime), interval)`, so it equals the interval for every interval of 30 days or more. Existing scopes have no stored idle timeout and get this default after the upgrade. The refresh token gets `exp = now + idleTimeout` at the token endpoint in `OID4VCIRefreshTokenProvider.getExpiration`. The credential gets `exp` from the later credential request plus the refresh interval in `OID4VCIssuerEndpoint.getVCToSign`. With equal values the refresh token never outlives the credential, so a refresh after credential expiry always fails. The documented cycle in `vc-issuer-configuration.adoc` is exactly that: the credential expires, then the wallet refreshes. Before this PR the refresh token lived for the full credential lifetime, so these wallets could refresh. The check at `OID4VCLoginProtocolFactory.java:466` and the form in `ScopeForm.tsx` also accept equality, and the error text says the token stays valid at least as long as the interval. That reason does not hold, because the credential expiry is counted from a later point than the token expiry. Only the `RANDOMIZE` and coarse `ROUND` time claim strategies hide this, because they move the credential expiry earlier. `testIdleTimeoutDefaultIsAtLeastRefreshInterval` pins the equal value. The comment at `OID4VCIssuerEndpoint.java:1828` still says the refresh token uses the full credential lifetime.
findings.fix: Derive the default with slack above the interval, for example `min(lifetime, max(30 days, 2 * interval))`, in `getRefreshIdleTimeoutInSeconds` and in `computeRefreshIdleTimeoutDefault`. State in the help text and the admin guide that an idle timeout equal to the interval leaves no time to refresh after expiry. Adjust the test and the stale comment in `getVCToSign`.

The validation now sees the same state that is persisted, so the checks are consistent. The reset itself existed before this PR. The PR makes partial updates a tested path with `testPartialUpdateValidatedAgainstStoredIdleTimeout` and now also accepts an update without a name. A changed configuration ID breaks refresh for issued tokens, because their authorization details name the old ID.

53864.headline: Restores pre-auth tx_code correctly, but case-sensitive text codes will trip up real users.
53864.summary: The PR lets the credential offer endpoint generate a six character `tx_code` for pre-authorized offers, returns it to the caller and adds the `tx_code` descriptor to the pre-authorized grant. The token endpoint checks the code before the pre-authorized code is consumed, the QR-only case is rejected, and the tests cover missing, wrong and correct codes. One usability problem should be fixed in this PR. The token endpoint compares the code case-sensitively against an upper-case alphabet that also contains look-alike characters.
53864.eudi: Issuers can again protect pre-authorized offers with a transaction code, as OpenID4VCI 1.0 intends for the pre-authorized code flow. Wallets get a `tx_code` object with `input_mode` and `length` as defined in Section 4.1.1, so they can prompt the holder for the code.
good: The `tx_code` check runs before `markPreAuthCodeAsUsed`, so a wrong code does not burn the offer.
A `tx_code` request with `type=qr` is rejected before any offer state is stored.
The grant now carries the `tx_code` descriptor, and the test asserts its `input_mode` and `length`.

findings.title: The generated text code is upper-case only but is compared case-sensitively and uses look-alike characters.
findings.impact: A holder who reads the code from an email or SMS and types it into a wallet text field in lower case, or confuses `O` with `0` or `I` with `1`, gets `Invalid TxCode` with no hint why.
findings.detail: `generateTxCode` draws from `A-Z0-9`, and the descriptor tells the wallet `input_mode` is `text`, so the wallet shows a normal keyboard. Mobile keyboards type lower case by default. `PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType` compares the submitted value with `MessageDigest.isEqual` on the raw bytes, so `ab12cd` fails against `AB12CD`. The alphabet also has `0`/`O` and `1`/`I`, which humans often mix up when they copy a code by hand. The holder can retry because a wrong code does not consume the offer, but the default offer lifespan is only a few minutes. Many holders will see a failed issuance before they work out the cause.
findings.fix: Normalize the submitted `tx_code` to upper case before the constant-time comparison in `PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType`. Drop the look-alike characters from `TX_CODE_ALPHABET`, for example by using the Crockford base32 set. You can also add a short `description` to the `TxCode` descriptor that tells the holder where to find the code.

53730.headline: Clean removal of the non-standard `credentials_offer_id`, with offer checks moved to token time.
53730.summary: The PR drops `credentials_offer_id` from OID4VC authorization details and from access and refresh tokens. Offer existence, expiry, target user and target client are now checked at the token endpoint, and the authorization code flow consumes the offer through a new `afterTokenResponseCreated` hook once the token response is built. Pre-authorized offers are no longer removed after issuance and stay until they expire, which the test comment calls deliberate and which is safe because `markPreAuthCodeAsUsed` keeps the code single use. The design is sound, the earlier review points are addressed, and I found only two follow-ups in code that the PR touches but did not break.
53730.eudi: Access and refresh tokens no longer carry the vendor field, and the token response was already free of it. An access token stays usable after its offer expires, so a wallet that requests the credential late is not rejected.
good: Offer consumption is deferred until the token response is built, and `testAuthCodeOffer_RemainsAvailableWhenTokenIssuanceFails` covers a failed exchange.
A missing or evicted offer now maps to `invalid_authorization_details` instead of a 500.

findings.detail: `TokenManager.attachAuthenticationSession` reuses a valid client session and only copies new notes on top. The old `client_request_param_issuer_state` note therefore stays. `getCredentialOfferState` falls back to that note, finds no offer because `afterTokenResponseCreated` removed it, and rejects the request. `AuthorizationCodeGrantType` calls `handleMissingAuthorizationDetails` for every token request without authorization details, so any later login of that client in the same SSO session is hit. Before this PR the same request failed once the first credential was issued. So the PR does not make the common flow worse, but the new consumption point is the natural place to fix it.

53978.headline: `claims_ref` works as described, but the setter, a docs gap and a stray revert remain.
53978.summary: The PR adds an optional `claims_ref` query parameter to `create-credential-offer`, stores it in `CredentialOfferState` and hands it to mappers through new `VCIssuanceContext` overloads of `setClaim`. The plumbing is correct, backward compatible and tested for both grant types. Nothing blocks the merge on correctness. Three small points should be fixed in this PR: the maintainer's open request for no setter and a short bound, a docs sentence that hides that holders can set the reference, and an unrelated line in `containers.adoc`.
53978.eudi: EUDI issuers that fill attestation claims from an external register get a record selector per offer for both flows. Their mapper must check the record against the authenticated user, because a holder can set the reference on a self issued offer.
good: The new `setClaim` overloads delegate to the old ones, so existing custom mappers keep working unchanged.
The reference stays server side and the integration test checks it reaches neither the wallet facing offer nor the credential.
Both flows are tested end to end, and batch issuance passes the same `offerState` to every credential.

findings.title: The docs do not say that a holder can set `claims_ref` without the `credential_offer_create` role.
findings.impact: A mapper author who reads that the issuing application supplies the reference may trust it, and then a logged in user can ask for `claims_ref=booking-43` on a self issued offer and get another customer's record in a signed credential.
findings.detail: `DefaultCredentialOfferProvider.validateTargetUser` skips the role check when the target user is the caller, and it is not called at all for an authorization code offer without a target user. `OID4VCIssuerEndpoint` copies `claimsRef` into the state at line 555 in all these cases. The mapper receives the reference and the user session, but not who created the offer. The docs deliberately put the check on the mapper, and that works for targeted and self issued offers because the mapper can compare the owner of the record with the session user. A role gate is therefore not required, and it would break portals that create self issued offers with the user's own token. The wording is the problem. It speaks of the issuing application and says existing offer authorization checks still apply, which reads as if only trusted callers can set the value.
findings.fix: State in the docs that any authenticated user can set `claims_ref` on a self issued or anonymous offer without the `credential_offer_create` role, so a mapper must treat the reference as untrusted input and check the record against the session user. If the maintainers want references to come only from trusted applications, require the role whenever `claims_ref` is present instead.

54096.headline: Completed flag works, but records from before the upgrade all read as incomplete attempts.
54096.summary: The PR adds a `completed` flag to issued credential records in local and federated storage. The credential endpoint sets the flag after a successful credential response. The flag is exposed through the Admin and Account REST APIs and survives export and import. The code path is correct and tested end to end. The documentation misleads for upgraded deployments and overstates what the issuer knows about delivery.
54096.eudi: EUDI issuers get a simple way to tell token requests that led to an issued credential apart from abandoned attempts. The flag only means Keycloak produced a credential response. It does not confirm that the wallet stored it.
good: The flag is set only after signing, encryption and nonce consumption succeed, so failed credential requests leave it false.
Federated users are handled through `UserStorageManager` with the same local then federated fallback as removal.
The new integration test checks the flag before and after a real credential request.

That is wrong for every row written before the upgrade. Such a row only turns true when the wallet next requests the credential with its existing token. An integration that cleans up or reports on incomplete attempts would act on credentials that holders actually have.

54034.headline: Spread object fields never reach mDoc credentials or the mandatory claim check.
54034.summary: The PR adds `OID4VCGraphQLClaimMapper`, which calls an admin configured GraphQL endpoint at issuance and writes the result into the credential subject. An object result is spread into one claim per field, and a hand written selection set parser lets issuer metadata list those fields. Validation is careful and the SD-JWT path works. But the spread fields skip `setClaimWithMetadataPrefix`, so mDoc credentials lose them and mandatory spread claims fail issuance.
54034.eudi: An issuer can now fill PID adjacent or attestation credentials from a backend register without custom code. The object mode is not yet usable for `mso_mdoc` attestations, and the lookup attribute must be one the holder cannot edit.
good: Issuer metadata is derived from the query selection set, so the advertised claims match what the mapper can emit.
Spread field names go through the same format aware reserved claim check as the configured claim name, including the `id` to `sub` normalization.
The mapper accepts only a single `query` operation, so a configured mutation cannot run during issuance.

findings.title: Spread object fields are never copied into the metadata prefixed claim map.
findings.impact: An admin who adds this mapper to an `mso_mdoc` scope with an object Response Path issues mDocs without any of the GraphQL fields, and an SD-JWT scope with Mandatory Claim enabled rejects every credential request.
findings.detail: The mapper does not override `setClaimWithMetadataPrefix`. The inherited version in `OID4VCMapper` copies only the value at `getClaimLookupPath()`, which is `[claim.name]`. In object mode the mapper writes `flightNumber`, `route` and so on, never `claim.name`, so nothing is copied. `OID4VCIssuerEndpoint` builds the mDoc subject only from `subjectClaimsWithMetadataPrefix` (line 1876), so the mDoc contains none of the fields that the metadata advertises under the namespace. For JSON formats, `validateRequestedClaimsArePresent` checks the metadata claims, now including each spread field, against the same prefixed map. With Mandatory Claim set, or when a wallet marks a spread claim mandatory in `authorization_details`, `ClaimsPathPointer.filterClaimsByAuthorizationDetails` throws `Mandatory claim not found` and the request fails with 400. The unit test for the mDoc exemption only calls `validate()` and `setClaim` and never runs this copy step. An automated review comment raised this earlier, and its thread was resolved after only the metadata paths were fixed.
findings.fix: Override `setClaimWithMetadataPrefix` so that in object mode it copies each resolved field name from the raw map to `prefixMetadataAttributePath(List.of(fieldName))`. Add an integration test that issues an `mso_mdoc` credential with an object Response Path, and one with Mandatory Claim enabled on an SD-JWT scope.

findings.title: A GraphQL `null` at the Response Path does not fail issuance.
findings.impact: A user who has no record in the backend gets `{"data":{"booking":null}}`, and Keycloak issues a credential with none of the advertised fields.
findings.detail: `navigatePath` returns Jackson's `NullNode` for a JSON `null`, not Java `null`. So the `node == null` guard does not fire. `NullNode` is neither an object nor an array, so the code falls through to `claims.put(claimName, unwrap(node))`, and `unwrap` returns `null`. Nullable lookup fields are the normal GraphQL answer for a missing record. A config that expects an object therefore writes a claim name that is not in the metadata, and the result is a signed credential without the data it is meant to carry.
findings.fix: Treat `node == null || node.isNull()` as no data and throw. Also decide whether `null` field values inside an object are omitted or rejected, and add a unit test for a `null` result.

54638.headline: Several JWT proofs sharing one key attestation now yield duplicate credentials per key.
54638.summary: The PR makes `JwtProofValidator` return every key in `attested_keys` and makes the endpoint issue one credential per returned key, which also takes effect for the unchanged `attestation` proof type. It resolves a numeric proof `kid` as a position in `attested_keys` and caps the batch by credentials instead of proofs. The fan out is clean, and each credential is built separately, so salts and generated ids stay unique. One case is new and wrong: several JWT proofs that carry the same key attestation each add the full attested key list, so the wallet gets duplicate credentials for the same keys.
54638.eudi: EUDI wallets that send one proof with a WUA listing several keys now receive one PID or attestation per key, which batch issuance and unlinkability under the ARF need. Wallets that send one JWT proof per key with the same WUA get linkable duplicates when `batch_size` is larger than the number of proofs, unless the scope sets `vc.key_attestation.proof_key_index` to 0, which rejects such requests anyway.
good: Proof validation now returns the keys and the endpoint does the binding, so one proof can fan out into several credentials without duplicating mapper logic.
Positional `kid` resolution still needs a signature from the resolved attested key, and an exact `kid` match takes precedence, so a positional `kid` cannot select a key the signer does not hold.
End to end tests cover multi key issuance for both the `jwt` and `attestation` proof types and check each `cnf` key in order.

findings.title: Several JWT proofs carrying the same key attestation produce duplicate credentials per attested key.

findings.detail: The endpoint calls `prepareCredentials` once per proof. `JwtProofValidator.validateSingleJwtProof` now returns the whole `attested_keys` list for every proof that has a `key_attestation`. Each proof therefore adds one context per attested key, and the cap at line 1064 only cuts the list at `batch_size`. Before this PR the same request produced one credential per proof, and it was the only way to get several credentials through JWT proofs when a key attestation is required, so existing wallets may still use it. The duplicates share a `cnf` key, so a wallet that stores them as separate one time credentials becomes linkable. The result is only right when the number of proofs equals `batch_size`, because the cut then keeps exactly the keys of the first proof. The new tests send one proof per request, so this case is not covered.
findings.fix: Skip keys that an earlier proof in the same request already bound, compared by key material or JWK thumbprint, before building the credential body. Keep collecting the verified nonce of a proof even when all its keys were already bound. Add an end to end test with two JWT proofs that carry the same attestation and assert two credentials with distinct `cnf` keys.

Callers that filtered `getClientScopesStream()` by name now use the new lookup, including the OID4VC user credential admin endpoints. I traced rename, removal, recreation under the same name, same transaction additions and concurrent renames through `RealmCacheSession` and found no path that returns a wrong or stale scope.
54656.eudi: Nothing changes for issuance or presentation. The OID4VC admin endpoints that create, update or revoke a user's credential by scope name keep the same semantics and no longer load every client scope of the realm.

54930.headline: The `CA:TRUE` check drops the issuing CA from metadata `x5c` when the root is omitted.
54930.summary: The PR lets the java-keystore provider load chains that do not end in a self-signed certificate. It also makes signed issuer metadata drop the topmost non-leaf certificate when it is self-signed or has `CA:TRUE`. The keystore change is sound and already lets admins leave out a non-self-signed trust anchor. The `CA:TRUE` check cannot tell an issuing CA from a trust anchor, so it removes a certificate that wallets need to build the path.
54930.eudi: Where the trusted list holds the root above an issuing CA, the configured chain `[leaf, issuing CA]` yields signed metadata with only the leaf, and wallets cannot verify the issuer. Where the trusted list holds the issuing CA itself, leaving that CA out of the keystore gives the same result without the heuristic and also keeps the SD-JWT VC and mdoc chains correct.
good: The keystore validation now checks the anchor's validity itself and validates only the path below the anchor, which is the correct PKIX setup.

findings.detail: `getBasicConstraints() >= 0` is true for every CA certificate. RFC 5280 Section 4.2.1.9 requires `cA` TRUE on each certificate that signs certificates, so the flag marks every intermediate and says nothing about which certificate the wallet trusts. The description presents the check as deliberate, but its reason does not hold because `CA:TRUE` does not identify an anchor. The PR's own V2 fixture is `[leaf, CA:TRUE intermediate]` with an external root left out, and the test expects only the leaf. A wallet that trusts that root gets no path to it. The only chain the check leaves intact is V4 with a non-CA intermediate, which path validation in RFC 5280 Section 6.1.4 rejects. `SdJwtCredentialSigner.addHaipX5cHeader` and `MdocCredential.requireCertificateChain` strip only self-signed certificates, so the same key yields a full chain in credentials and a truncated chain in metadata. The keystore change in this PR already covers a non-self-signed anchor. The admin leaves it out, as the docs require for SD-JWT VCs, and a lone `[leaf]` now loads. An anchor that is not self-signed and sits above an issuing CA has no single keystore layout that is right for both metadata and credentials.

54895.headline: Small backward compatible SPI hook that lets well-known providers pick their media type.
54895.summary: The PR adds a default `getMediaType()` to `WellKnownProvider` and uses it in `RealmsResource.getWellKnownResponse`. It also removes `@Produces` from both GET well-known methods so that a provider type such as `application/entity-statement+jwt` no longer gets a 406. Providers that return `null` keep the old String to `application/jwt` and object to `application/json` inference, so OIDC, UMA, OAuth2 and both OID4VCI providers return the same types as before. The change is minimal and the tests cover both endpoints and the unchanged default.
54895.eudi: OID4VCI issuer metadata keeps its JSON default and its signed `application/jwt` variant from OID4VCI 1.0 Section 12.2.2 unchanged. The hook makes it possible to serve OpenID Federation entity configurations with the correct media type, which EUDI trust setups based on federation need.
good: The PR uses a default interface method instead of special casing provider classes in `RealmsResource`, so existing and third party providers keep working.
The PR states the one behaviour change openly. An unrelated `Accept` type now gets the document instead of a 406, which no metadata spec forbids.
The tests cover both the realm path and the server metadata path, with `*/*` and with the provider's own media type.

54854.headline: Adds OIDC Core conformance suites with careful retries and only small follow-ups remain.
54854.summary: The PR runs the OpenID Connect Core Config, Basic, Implicit, Hybrid, Form Post and Dynamic certification plans against Keycloak as three new jobs of the manual conformance workflow. It adds opt-in retries with a fresh suite alias for every attempt, stops a failed module before it runs again, and tunnels Keycloak's outgoing requests to the suite's internal host. All changes are test code, the points from the review by lhanusov are addressed, and the new runner parts have focused unit tests. I found nothing that must change before merge.
54854.eudi: The PR changes no production code, so EUDI deployments are not affected. The OID4VCI and OID4VP tests only see the broader login page pattern and the stop of a failed module, and they still run without retries.
good: Retries are opt-in for the OIDC tests, and every attempt uses its own suite alias and redirect URI, so a late callback cannot reach another run.
A failed module is stopped and awaited before a retry, and a failed stop ends the test instead of retrying.
`SuiteTunnel`, `ConformanceAttempts` and the cleanup in `ConformanceApiClient` have unit tests against fakes that cover shutdown, reset and timeout paths.

55075.headline: Non-string claims now reach session notes safely, with only a small object matching nit.
55075.summary: The PR lets the OIDC `ClaimToUserSessionNoteMapper` store array, object, number and boolean claims as session notes. Arrays are joined with a comma, objects are stored as JSON and an empty configured value stores any claim. UserInfo arrays keep all elements through a new opt-in flag on `getJsonValue`, and a missing field before an array index no longer throws. String claims, regex mode and token precedence behave as before, and the unit tests cover the new paths well.
55075.eudi: This is the OIDC brokering mapper and does not touch credential issuance or presentation. EUDI deployments are only affected if they broker an external OIDC IdP and forward its claims to clients.
good: The `keepArrays` flag is opt-in, so the other JSON and claim mappers keep their old UserInfo behaviour.
The null guard before `currentNode.isArray()` fixes a `NullPointerException` that any mapper could hit with a path such as `missing[0]`.
Regex mode stays limited to string claims, which avoids patterns that match serialized arrays or objects by accident.

findings.title: Object claims are matched by comparing serialized JSON strings.
findings.impact: An admin who configures `{"locality": "London"}` with a space, or with the keys in another order than the IdP sends them, never gets the note and sees no error.
findings.detail: `claimValues` turns every element into a string before `valueEquals` runs, so an object claim only matches when the configured text is byte for byte the compact JSON that Jackson writes. `AbstractClaimMapper.valueEquals` already compares a `JsonNode` by parsing the configured value and comparing trees, which ignores whitespace and key order.
findings.fix: For object and nested array elements, parse the configured value with `JsonSerialization.readValue(value, JsonNode.class)` and compare the trees. Keep the text comparison for strings, numbers and booleans, because a tree comparison would stop a plain value such as `user` from matching. Use the string form only when the note is stored.

changes: The line of the object matching nit moved from 182 to 163, because line 182 in the checkout is the regex check and the equality match is on line 163.

The fix of the object matching nit now limits the tree comparison to object and nested array elements, because `valueEquals(value, element)` on a text node fails to parse a plain value such as `user` and would break string matching.

55191.headline: Correct and safe to merge, but the logged offer nonce still returns the pre-authorized code.
55191.summary: The PR drops the debug line in `getCredentialOffer` that ran `JsonSerialization.valueAsString(credOffer)` and so printed the `grants` map with the `pre-authorized_code`. It also replaces the issuance debug line with the configuration id, the format and the claim names. At this commit `VerifiableCredential` has no `toString()`, so the old issuance line printed only an object identity, and the new line is more useful while still keeping values out. The change is correct and nothing in it must change, but the `Found credential offer` line that stays logs a nonce that returns the same code, so the leak is only fully closed by a follow-up.
55191.eudi: EUDI issuers that run with debug logging no longer write the pre-authorized code itself in the offer response line. The offer nonce is still logged and returns the same code while the offer is live.
good: The offer line is removed rather than redacted, so no hand built replacement has to read the `grants` map.
The new issuance line logs claim names without values, which helps when debugging mappers.
The description states clearly which nearby log lines are out of scope and asks for a maintainer view.

findings.title: The offer nonce in the debug log still gives access to the pre-authorized code.
findings.impact: Anyone who can read issuer debug logs can call the offer endpoint with the logged nonce while the offer is live, read the pre-authorized code and redeem it when no `tx_code` is required.
findings.detail: The `Stored credential offer state` line at 587 and the `Found credential offer` line at 696 log `offerState.getNonce()`. `CredentialOfferState` builds that value as the random secret plus the offer id, and `DefaultCredentialOfferStorage.getOfferStateByNonce` accepts exactly that string. `getCredentialOffer` then returns the full offer with the `pre-authorized_code`, and the lookup is repeatable until the offer expires or the credential is issued. The stored line is written when the offer is created, before the wallet scans the QR code, so the window is the whole offer lifetime. The author left the nonce out because the issue does not name it. That reason does not hold for the goal in the PR title, because the line at 696 runs in the same request as the removed line and hands the same log reader the nonce that returns the same code. The gap is older than the PR and the PR does not make it worse, so it is a follow-up. The raw request payload at line 790 can stay, because it carries no code and no claim values, and replaying it needs the access token that is checked at line 802 and is not in the payload.
findings.fix: In a follow-up, log `offerState.getCredentialsOfferId()` instead of the nonce in both lines. The offer id alone is not accepted by the offer endpoint and is already logged at lines 921 and 950.
